## About this series
This series is adapted from my 2017 lecture notes, *Introduction to Statistical Tests* ([original PDF](/assets/docs/statests.pdf)). [Part 7](../stats-7-chi-square/index.qmd) finished the tests for counts. This last part returns to measurements and to the assumption most tests rest on: normality.
:::

## When the data are not normal

Many of the tests we met in Parts 3 to 5 assume that the data, or their residuals, are roughly normal. Real measurements are often not. Concentrations, counts, incomes and reaction times tend to be **right-skewed**: most values are small, and a few are very large. The mean is dragged towards the tail (Part 1), and a $t$-test run on such data can mislead.

You have two options: use a non-parametric test, as we did throughout the series, or **transform** the variable so that the result is closer to normal and then use the parametric test. Sometimes you can restore normality with a simple function.

```{r setup}
library(ggplot2)

# A shared look for the figures in this series
accent <- "#8c2f39"; gold <- "#b08d4a"; ink <- "#5d6070"
theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
    theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#FFFDF8", colour = NA),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "#EEEAE0", linewidth = 0.3),
          plot.title.position = "plot")
)
```

## A ladder of transformations

Take serum cortisol levels in 200 ewes. The distribution is strongly right-skewed:

```{r data}
set.seed(8)
cortisol <- rlnorm(200, meanlog = 3, sdlog = 0.6)   # nmol/L
c(mean = mean(cortisol), median = median(cortisol))
shapiro.test(cortisol)$p.value
```

The mean is well above the median, which is the signature of right skew, and Shapiro–Wilk rejects normality decisively. The standard remedies form a "ladder of powers": the further down the ladder, the stronger the squeeze on the long right tail (up to a point).

| Transformation | R | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| none | `x` | symmetric data |
| square root | `sqrt(x)` | mild right skew, counts |
| logarithm | `log(x)` | strong right skew, positive data growing by ratios |
| reciprocal | `1 / x` | very strong right skew, such as waiting times |

For *left*-skewed data we go the other way, up the ladder (for example `x^2`), or reflect the variable first (`max(x) + 1 - x`) and then apply one of the transformations above.

```{r ladder}
#| fig-alt: "Four histograms of the cortisol data: raw, square root, log, and reciprocal. Raw is strongly right-skewed, the square root less so, the log is roughly symmetric, and the reciprocal is again right-skewed."
versions <- list(raw = cortisol, `square root` = sqrt(cortisol),
                 log = log(cortisol), reciprocal = 1 / cortisol)

W <- sapply(versions, function(v) unname(shapiro.test(v)$statistic))
long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(versions), function(nm)
  data.frame(version = sprintf("%s (W = %.3f)", nm, W[nm]), value = versions[[nm]])))
long$version <- factor(long$version, levels = unique(long$version))

ggplot(long, aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#d8cfba", colour = "#FFFDF8") +
  facet_wrap(~ version, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Climbing down the ladder of powers",
       subtitle = "W is the Shapiro-Wilk statistic: closer to 1 means closer to normal")
```

The raw data are skewed, the square root helps but leaves a tail, and the logarithm makes the distribution nearly symmetric. The reciprocal does not help at all here. This is a general lesson: a transformation has to match the shape of the skew, and the ladder is a guide, not a guarantee. The logarithm is the right one in this case, which is no accident, because the data were generated as log-normal: by definition, a variable is log-normal if its logarithm is normal (and so is the logarithm of its reciprocal, which is why the reciprocal is no better than the raw data). Biological quantities that arise from many multiplicative effects often behave this way.

### Letting the data choose: Box–Cox

Rather than trying transformations by hand, the **Box–Cox** family estimates the power $\lambda$ that makes the data most nearly normal ($\lambda = 1$ is no change, $0.5$ the square root, $0$ the logarithm, $-1$ the reciprocal):

```{r boxcox}
bc <- MASS::boxcox(lm(cortisol ~ 1), lambda = seq(-1, 1.5, 0.05), plotit = FALSE)
lambda <- bc$x[which.max(bc$y)]
lambda
```

The estimate is close to zero: the data are asking for a logarithm. A $\lambda$ near a "round" value like 0, 0.5 or $-1$ is best rounded to that value, since it keeps the result interpretable.

## Checking the result

A transformed variable should pass the same checks as any other. A Q–Q plot before and after shows the improvement:

```{r qq}
#| fig-alt: "Two Q-Q plots. The raw cortisol values curve upwards away from the line at the right end; the logged values follow the line closely."
qq <- rbind(data.frame(version = "raw", x = cortisol),
            data.frame(version = "log", x = log(cortisol)))
qq$version <- factor(qq$version, levels = c("raw", "log"))

ggplot(qq, aes(sample = x)) +
  stat_qq(colour = accent, alpha = 0.7) +
  stat_qq_line(colour = ink) +
  facet_wrap(~ version, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Sample quantiles")

shapiro.test(log(cortisol))$p.value
```

## What a transformation costs

Transforming is not free, and a few cautions apply:

* **Interpretation changes.** A $t$-test on log-transformed values compares means *on the log scale*, which correspond to **geometric means** on the original scale. That is often just what you want for ratios (a 20% increase), but report it. Back-transform estimates and confidence limits with `exp()`:

```{r backtransform}
tt <- t.test(log(cortisol))
c(estimate = exp(unname(tt$estimate)),
  lower    = exp(tt$conf.int[1]),
  upper    = exp(tt$conf.int[2]))   # geometric mean, with its 95% CI
```

* **Zeros break logs.** `log(0)` is minus infinity. If zeros are real, a common (though ad hoc) fix is `log1p(x)`, or `log(x + c)` with a small constant. Think about what the zeros mean before reaching for it.
* **Do not shop for significance.** Choose the transformation by looking at the *distribution* of the variable, not by trying several and keeping the one that gives the smallest p-value.
* **Transformation is not always the right tool.** Counts are better modelled directly, with Poisson or negative-binomial regression, than forced into normality. And when a single transformation cannot rescue the data, the non-parametric tests of this series remain available.

## The series in one page

Over eight parts we went from "what is a mean?" to a toolbox of tests. A compact map:

| Question | Data | Assumptions hold | Otherwise |
|---|---|---|---|
| One sample against a value | measurements | one-sample $t$-test | Wilcoxon signed-rank |
| Two independent samples | measurements | Welch's $t$-test | Wilcoxon rank-sum (Mann–Whitney) |
| Two paired samples | measurements | paired $t$-test | Wilcoxon signed-rank on differences |
| Three or more samples | measurements | ANOVA, then Tukey | Kruskal–Wallis, then pairwise Wilcoxon (Holm) |
| Equal variances | measurements | Levene (robust), Bartlett | |
| Normality | measurements | Shapiro–Wilk plus a Q–Q plot | |
| One or several proportions | counts | `prop.test` | `binom.test`, Fisher's exact test |
| Fit to a distribution | counts | `chisq.test(x, p = ...)` | |
| Independence of two categories | counts | `chisq.test(table)` | Fisher's exact test |

A few habits matter more than any single test. Plot your data first. State the null hypothesis before you compute anything. Report **effect sizes and confidence intervals**, not just p-values. And remember that "not significant" means *not enough evidence*, which is not the same as *no effect*.

Thank you for reading this series. It began as a set of lecture notes from 2017 and I enjoyed bringing it up to date. If you spot a mistake, or want a topic covered next (regression and linear models are the obvious sequel), do get in touch.
